title: SLA & Isolation Asks Framework for Procurement
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, procurement‑ready framing doc for sales and solutions to use when negotiating dedicated capacity deals. Focus: clear asks and messaging around SLA guarantees, workload isolation, predictable throughput, and commercial tradeoffs. Keep this in your pocket for RFP responses, procurement calls, and legal term drafts.

Audience and intent
- Primary: procurement leads, platform architects, infra buyers, legal counsel at target accounts.
- Secondary: internal AE/SEs who need crisp asks and fallback language.
- Intent: shorten procurement cycles by presenting a concrete, low‑ambiguity offer that balances customer risk concerns with Redwood’s operational model.

Core positioning lines to use up‑front
- "Dedicated capacity gives you deterministic throughput and tail‑latency with infrastructure isolation and contractual SLAs — so your product behaves the same at 10k qps as it does in staging."
- "We treat isolation as both a performance and compliance boundary: compute pools, network controls, and audit trails are dedicated to your contract, not shared across tenants."
- "Our SLA ties availability to throughput and tail latency, with predefined credit mechanics and clear escalation paths so you can validate SLOs in production."

Procurement Ask Checklist (what we propose to include in term sheet)
- Availability: 99.9% per month for the serving endpoint(s) measured at route level (availability excludes scheduled maintenance windows with >72h notice).
- Tail latency: p99 response time SLO (configurable by model class) with credits triggered after two consecutive breach days; sample targets: p99 < 800ms for short prompt workloads (<512 tokens), p99 < 2s for long‑context workloads (>2k tokens).
- Throughput guarantees: committed tokens/sec (or concurrent requests) per pool with burst pool access at measured throttling rates. Provide a baseline and burst policy (e.g., 25% burstable capacity sustained for 10 minutes).
- Isolation guarantees: dedicated GPU pool, isolated internal network (VPC peering or Private Connect), tenant‑specific KV caches, and no noisy‑neighbor scheduling on the reserved nodes.
- Data controls: customer keys for encryption at rest (KMS/HSM), detailed audit logs (request/response hashes, who/when), optional log redaction, and data retention windows per customer requirement.
- MTTR / Escalation: target mean time to restore for critical incidents (e.g., 2 hours), named escalation contact and 24/7 pager coverage for P1 incidents as part of enterprise tier.
- Degraded mode / fallbacks: automatic graceful fallback policy to a lower‑cost/compatible model variant with explicit quality regression windows, and a separate SLA for fallback availability.
- Capacity reporting & telemetry: daily token/latency reports and API access to per‑route metrics; monthly capacity reconciliation and a dashboard export for finance.
- Credits and remedies: clearly defined credit schedule (e.g., 5% of monthly committed fee for SLA breach on availability, sliding scale for repeat breaches).
- Termination & exit: data export tooling, model weights not included (if private), and a 90‑day data handover commitment with tooling/scripted exports.

Negotiation framing (scripts & quick responses)
- Procurement: "We understand you need contractable availability & isolation — we can lock to a 99.9% availability SLA, with clearly defined maintenance windows and credits. For predictable throughput, we’ll define committed tokens/sec and an agreed burst policy. What throughput number would you measure as success for your initial rollout?"
- Legal: "We can accept a fixed credit ladder for availability and latency breaches, but we need to preserve our right to scheduled maintenance with 72h notice and an exclusion for customer‑induced outages. Can you share your standard critical incident steps so we can map escalation overlap?"
- Engineering / Platform buyer: "We’ll provide dedicated GPU pools, per‑tenant KV caches, and VPC connectivity. For on‑prem or VPC deployments we’ll include a handover runbook and a 30‑day operational co‑pilot period. Which isolation controls matter most for your audit team?"

Commercial levers and configuration options to offer
- Commit length: 12/24/36 month tiers with increasing uptime/latency SLOs and discounts for longer commits.
- Capacity units: sold as committed tokens/sec, reserved vGPU count, or reserved concurrency slots depending on buyer preference.
- Burst buckets: optional paid burst credits or contained burst with autoscaling up to a cap.
- Quality tiers: primary model family (verified by Redwood) vs cost‑optimized quantized variants; SLA differs for quantized variants (explicitly call out model quality/regression risk).
- Professional services add‑on: deployment runbook, on‑site kickoff, monthly optimization workshops, and a dedicated solutions engineer during onboarding.

Competitive analysis shorthand (use on calls; avoid deep public dimpling)
- Large cloud managed endpoints: Pros = easy network integration, large capacity; Cons = multi‑tenant noisy neighbor risk in managed offerings, less LLM specialization, limited rollback/rollout tooling tuned for model families.
- LLM API pureplay vendors: Pros = simple pricing and often best in class for latest models; Cons = less visibility into token economics, limited dedicated isolation options and enterprise network features.
- Self‑hosted inference infra providers: Pros = full control and potential lower cost at scale; Cons = operational burden, slow to tune kernels/quantization and a longer time to value.
- Redwood angle: we are the middle path — unified runtime optimized for inference, plus managed operations, contractual isolation, and tooling for rollouts/quality checks. Differentiate on operational guarantees and integrated fallback/rollout controls.

SLA technical appendix (what eng expects in contract)
- Definition of measurement points: per-route ingress measured at edge proxy, p99 measured over 1‑minute sliding windows, aggregated daily.
- Exclusions: customer traffic shaping, malformed requests, 3rd‑party provider outages (cloud provider network), scheduled maintenance with >=72 hours notice.
- Verification: monthly automated verification test harness (customer can opt‑in to run blackbox probes against routes), sample golden prompts and acceptance criteria for latency/throughput validation.

Red flags and tradeoffs to watch for
- Procurement asks for unlimited burst with no pricing: push back — unlimited burst undermines predictability and cost. Offer time‑bounded bursts or paid burst credits.
- Legal wanting severe SLA credit caps or unilateral termination: escalate to revenue/legal for carveouts and risk adjustments.
- Requests for model weight delivery: clarify that weights are not part of hosted/dedicated offerings; offer a private/OEM package under a separate enterprise arrangement.

Next steps for AE/SE
- Use this doc as the first attachment for procurement responses.
- Spin a short one‑pager (customer friendly) with the top 6 asks (availability, tail latency, throughput, isolation, data controls, credits) for each RFP.
- Add to Jira GTMP-1287 any customer‑specific deviations and tag legal review.

Notes / working questions (open)
- Do we want a hard numeric p99 baseline in all term sheets or make it model/class configurable? (Action: Product to propose defaults per model family)
- Should we publish a public Dedicated SLA reference page for self‑serve enterprise customers? (Action: Marketing + Docs)

References and bookmarks

- Example ticket: GTMP‑1287 (procurement exceptions tracker)
- Internal thread: slack:#sales‑dedicated (see 2026‑01‑26 thread about p99 targets)

Author notes
- Drafted for rapid reuse; keep this page short and copyable into term sheets. This is intentionally pragmatic — the legal team will convert language into binding contract text.
- Feedback welcome from Legal and Product on measurement definitions and breach mechanics.

---
End of doc.
